sources.name: Jax Caldera
sources.quote: Honestly, I see people push through more than they go in. It's not stubbornness — it's that the hospital's not close, and a lot of folks here work jobs where taking a day off means losing pay or losing a shift. I've watched neighbors ride out fevers with herbal tea and a heating pad because the alternative was a bill they couldn't explain. The ones who do go in are usually past the point of choice. That's the part that gets me — by the time someone here decides to see a doctor, it's not a precaution anymore, it's an emergency.

sources.name: Akua Adeyemi
sources.quote: I see it in the little things, honestly. A bottle of cough syrup moved from the bathroom to the kitchen counter, so it's right there where someone'll remember it. Or a chair pulled up by the window, where someone's been sitting a long time, just watching the street. Sometimes the whole house gets rearranged — the bed moved downstairs, or the living room turned into a bedroom, because stairs got too hard. You don't have to ask. You just see it.

sources.name: Yu Zen
sources.quote: When I was in that hospital bed after my accident, I learned something about who shows up for you. It's not the building with the big sign — it's the people. Chinatown's got the most sick right now, and I know that neighborhood doesn't have the hospital footprint the rest of us take for granted. But I've seen how those communities work — the families, the shopkeepers, the elders checking on each other. That's where the caring happens when the beds are full. I think about that every morning now when I walk past the hospital cart for coffee. The city's at 70 beds, all full — that's not a number to me anymore. That's 70 people hoping someone shows up for them the way my family showed up for me.
